1:
Two full years pass before anything moves, and the reckoning of them is not settled. Gill notes it is not clear whether the count runs from Joseph's imprisonment or from the butler's release, and judges the latter more probable, since it binds this chapter to the one before. Clarke reads the Hebrew as two years of days, two complete solar revolutions after the events last told. Calvin takes the same phrase for full and entire years and makes the delay the point: God exercised his servant not by long waiting only but by taking every human ground of hope away from him. What anxiety oppressed the holy man in that time, he says, each of us may guess from his own feeling, since we are so tender and effeminate that we can scarcely bear to be put off for a short while. Henry turns the delay into a lesson. We have need of patience, not only bearing but waiting patience; there is a time set for the deliverance of God's people, and though it seem to tarry it will prove, when it comes, to have been the best time.

The dreams themselves draw out the Egyptology. Kine and ears alike rise from the river, and Ellicott explains why: no rain falls in Egypt, so its fertility depends wholly on the Nile's overflow, and the cow was the Egyptian symbol of the earth and of agriculture, the cows sacred to Isis being seven in number. Clarke wants the animal more particular still, insisting it must be the hippopotamus, since coming up out of the river and feeding in the field characterises that creature alone. The meadow, Ellicott says, is properly marsh-grass, the rank herbage of the Nile banks, a word found only here and in one other place. The seven ears on one stalk he identifies as the Egyptian wheat that bears several heads on a single stem, and he sets aside the old report that Egyptians thought it shameful to eat wheat, since the temple paintings show it was the main crop and its cultivation held in honour. Keil and Delitzsch add only that the vision lay so close to reality that Pharaoh perceived it was a dream only on waking.

On the blasting east wind Clarke is fullest. Blasting, smut, mildew and locust are all laid to that wind, and in Egypt it is peculiarly destructive because it comes through the parched deserts of Arabia. He reports a traveller's account of the simoom on the road to Syene: the guide crying out to fall on their faces, a purple haze not twenty yards broad and twelve feet high moving fast over the sand, the whole company lying flat as dead until it had blown over, and the narrator carrying an asthmatic complaint for two years after. Ellicott is more cautious, observing that Egypt's winds are generally north or south and that the south-eastern Chamsin may be meant, Hebrew having names for only the four chief winds.

Calvin draws the doctrine. God sometimes deigns to present his oracles even to unbelieving and profane men, and it was a singular honour that Pharaoh should be instructed about an event fourteen years off. Yet the limit is marked: the doctrine that leads to the hope of eternal life belongs to the Church, while the children of this world are taught only incidentally about the present life, and the interpretation of the oracle had to be sought elsewhere. The doubling of the dream he explains as God's ordinary method, repeating what he has delivered both to rouse the hearer to inquiry and to add light, the ears of corn agreeing better with the thing signified than the cattle did. Gill and Henry both stop at the strangeness of it, that tame cattle should devour their own kind, which was never known.
8:
By morning the dream will not leave him. Gill says the images stood before Pharaoh awake as they had asleep, so that he could have no ease until he knew their meaning; Wesley agrees that it cannot but put a man into a concern to receive any extraordinary message from heaven. Calvin makes the disquiet itself evidential — a sting was left in Pharaoh's heart that he might know he had to deal with God, the anxiety serving as an inward seal to authenticate the dream.

The men he calls in are described with some care. Keil and Delitzsch derive the word from a stylus and identify them with the sacred scribes, men of the priestly caste who kept the hieroglyphic writings, astrology, the interpretation of dreams, magic and conjuring, and were reckoned masters of secret arts. Clarke thinks the term more likely Egyptian than Hebrew, its etymology therefore lost with the art of reading hieroglyphs itself. Of the wise men he gives an admiring account borrowed from the ancients: men who gave their whole lives to the contemplation of divine things, to the stars, to self-purification, arithmetic and geometry, and to singing hymns; it was probably among these that Pythagoras conversed, and from them that he took the modest name of philosopher, a lover of wisdom. Ellicott is drier. The sacred scribes did possess real knowledge, but in antiquity real knowledge was habitually dressed in a claim to occult acquaintance with the secrets of gods and nature, which the superstition of the multitude made easy to maintain; it was divination and astrology, not science, that brought them wealth and honour.

Their failure is variously read. Ellicott supposes many did attempt an interpretation, but so imperfectly that Pharaoh's mind was not satisfied. Keil and Delitzsch find the failure ironical, since the clue lay in Egypt's own religious symbols — the cow stood for the earth, for agriculture and for food, and the Nile's overflow was the source of the land's fertility. Wesley says simply that the rules of their art failed them, which made Joseph's performance by the Spirit of God the more admirable. Calvin goes furthest: Pharaoh deserved to lose the benefit of the revelation by running to imposters, and it is the folly of the human mind to gather to itself teachers of error. That he thought them true prophets excuses nothing, since he voluntarily closed his eyes. God therefore struck the boasters dumb, so that a credulous king who would gladly have been deluded could not even be given a plausible answer — a mercy, Calvin says, for the Lord provides best when he removes the incitements of error from those who wish to be deceived.

Then the butler speaks. Henry judges the confession more a compliment to Pharaoh than any gratitude to Joseph, but allows that remembering one's faults and repenting late is better than never. Clarke is harsher, holding it impossible the man could ever have forgotten, only inconvenient to remember until remembering served his own interest — a courtier who had been in the same prison himself and found it convenient to forget the poor friendless Hebrew slave. Calvin reads the words differently again: not a confession of ingratitude but a necessary preface, since the minds of kings are sensitive and the butler had to acknowledge his imprisonment just, lest Pharaoh suspect a grudge. Behind it all Calvin sees the true design — God pitied Egypt not for the king's sake nor the country's, but that Joseph might come out of prison and that in the famine bread might be found for his Church, which he esteemed more highly than ten worlds. Henry draws the same providence from the delay: had the butler procured a release two years earlier, Joseph would probably have gone home to the land of the Hebrews, and been neither so blessed himself nor such a blessing to his family.
14:
The summons is instant, and the small details of the toilet get more attention than the haste. Gill has Pharaoh sending messengers with orders to loose him and let him go free. Clarke supposes Joseph had let his beard grow through the imprisonment and now merely trimmed it, doubting that either Egyptians or Hebrews shaved in our sense of the word, and reasons that the change of raiment came out of the king's wardrobe, since a prisoner could have had no changes of his own. Ellicott turns the same clause into evidence: the Egyptians let hair and beard grow only in mourning, and on the monuments a beard marks a captive or a man of low condition, whereas in Palestine it was a manly ornament — so Joseph would leave his untrimmed in prison and take it off before the king. Calvin guessed the opposite, that a nation so studious of elegance would rather have nourished its hair, and reads the shaving simply as the last removal of shame. The servant of God, he says, lay in filth to the very day of his deliverance.

Calvin sees more in the summons than urgency. In this proud king, as in a glass, we may see what necessity can effect. Prosperous men will scarcely condescend to hear those they hold true prophets, still less strangers; Pharaoh's obstinacy had first to be subdued before he would send for a Hebrew and accept him as master and instructor. The same preparation, Calvin insists, is needed by the elect, who never become docile until the pride of the flesh is laid low. When Pharaoh then offers himself as a disciple, Calvin calls it a constrained humility, yet recorded for our sake, so that when the opportunity of learning is put before us we may not refuse to honour the gifts of the Spirit. Ellicott passes on Abravanel's observation that every suffering of Joseph had its exact recompense: it was for dreams that his brethren hated him, and by dreams that he was exalted; they stripped him of his coat and the Egyptians clothed him in fine linen; they sold him into slavery, and in Egypt he was made lord.

Joseph's disclaimer is where the weight falls. Gill hears in it great modesty, a refusal to arrogate any such skill to himself, since what he had was a gift of God and wholly dependent on what God was pleased to reveal. Clarke presses the Hebrew: the phrase is without me, independently of me — I am not essential to thy comfort, God himself has thee under his care — and finds in the promised answer of peace a word for prosperity, however ominous the dreams might appear. Wesley draws the double lesson, that Joseph gives honour to God, since great gifts appear most graceful when their holders use them humbly and give the praise away, and that he shows hearty good-will to Pharaoh in supposing the interpretation would be an answer of peace. Calvin gives the sentence its sharpest reading. Knowing he was speaking with a heathen addicted to superstition, Joseph wanted above all to give God the glory due to him, as if to say that he could do nothing in the matter and would offer nothing as from himself, God alone being the interpreter of his own secret. And he distinguishes the promise of peace from the prophecy: Joseph did not yet know what the oracle would be, so could not undertake a happy issue, and the word is a prayer rather than a prediction, added out of the kindly feeling of his heart. The lesson Calvin takes home is that we should honour the grace of God even among unbelievers, and where they shut the door against the whole doctrine of piety, at least endeavour to instil some drops of it; for the first step of wisdom is to ascribe nothing to ourselves.
17:
Pharaoh tells the dream over again, and the commentators notice that he tells it differently. Gill observes that the account is fuller than the first, and Ellicott makes the point exactly: the king's recital is longer than the narrative, and adds the impressions the sight left on him — that he never beheld such wretched cattle in Egypt, and that after devouring the fat ones they were as ill-favoured as before. The one entirely new term describes the bad ears, and it stands alone in the whole of scripture. Gill collects the rabbinic attempts on it: small or little, void and empty husk with no grain, mere shadows of ears, or, from a Syriac word for rock, dry as stone. Ellicott lands in the same place: the word means stony, the grains shrivelled hard like grit.

Henry and Clarke both stop at the river. Egypt has no rain, so the plenty of the year hangs on the inundation, and it is measured: Henry gives fifteen or sixteen cubits for plenty, twelve or thirteen for scarcity. Clarke draws the inference the dream itself invites — the fat kine and the lean came up out of the same river, which at a stroke shows the cause of both, since the good years must be owing to an extraordinary overflow and the bad to a partial failure or none at all. Henry will not let the second causes stand alone: see how many ways Providence has of dispensing its gifts, yet our dependence is the same upon the first Cause, who makes every creature to us what it is, be it rain or river.

On the doubling of the dream Henry sees a design in the pairing. The two visions mean one thing, and the repetition marks the certainty, the nearness and the importance of the event; yet they are not simply duplicates, since they answer to the two things in which men most feel plenty and want, the kine standing for grass and the cattle it feeds, the ears for the corn that serves man. From this he draws the ordinary use: after great plenty may come great scarcity, and we must learn how to want as well as how to abound. He adds a note for rulers: God revealed this beforehand to Pharaoh, who as king was to be the father of his country and provide for it, and magistrates are called shepherds, whose care must be not only to rule but to feed.

Clarke pauses over the detail that troubled Pharaoh most, that the lean kine were no better for their meal. Nothing, he says, could more powerfully mark the severity of the famine than creatures eating each other and remaining as wretched as before; and he offers a physical explanation, that want sharpens the appetite and hurries food through the body before its nourishment can be absorbed. Calvin reads the same clause as testimony rather than physiology: God meant to show that the dearth would be so great that the people, instead of being nourished by the abundance gathered together, would be famished and drag on a miserable existence.

The rest of Calvin's comment is given to the grammar of Joseph's preface. Joseph does not say that God will announce beforehand what may happen from some other quarter, but that God shows what he himself is about to do — and from that small turn Calvin argues a large case. God does not idly contemplate the chance issue of things, as most philosophers vainly talk, but determines at his own will what shall happen; in foretelling he does not read from the tables of fate, like the Apollo of the poets, but declares that whatever comes will be his own work. So whenever the earth is barren, whether frost or drought or hail be the visible cause, the whole result is directed by the counsel of God.
25:
The interpretation begins by collapsing the two visions into one. Gill puts it plainly: though there were two distinct dreams under different images, the sense was the same, and one interpretation would serve for both. Clarke fastens on the words that follow, that God has shown Pharaoh what he is about to do. The ordinary cause of Egyptian plenty or want is the river, but its inundations are under God's direction, and the dreams were sent not merely to give notice of the coming abundance and scarcity but to show that circumstances which look entirely fortuitous are under an overruling providence.

The measurements return, and here they are given in full. Gill says the seven good years meant not sufficiency merely but abundance even to luxury, such as followed when the Nile rose to sixteen cubits, and that though the overflow is a natural cause it was owing to God, since no other account can be given of its rising so for seven years together; the famine likewise came of the river failing its banks, twelve cubits being enough to bring one on. Clarke sets out the whole ancient scale. Sixteen cubits is the just increase; a lesser flood does not water all the ground, and a greater is too slow in running off, so that in the one case the soil is not saturated and in the other seed-time is lost. Twelve cubits and the province feels famine; thirteen still goes hungry; fourteen brings rejoicing, fifteen security, sixteen all the luxuries of life. He adds that the scale still held in his own day, and that a rise to eighteen cubits prevents sowing in season and produces a famine as certainly as no overflow at all.

Wesley takes the sequence for a mercy. See the goodness of God in sending the seven years of plenty before those of famine, that provision might be made accordingly; and see how wisely Providence, that great housekeeper, has ordered the affairs of this numerous family from the beginning, for the produce of the earth is sometimes more and sometimes less, yet taking one time with another what was miraculous in the manna is ordinarily verified in the common course of things, and he that gathers much has nothing over while he that gathers little has no lack. Against that he sets the other side of the account. The great increase of the plenteous years was quite lost and swallowed up in the famine, and the overplus, which had seemed very much, did but just serve to keep men alive — which is what he means by the perishing nature of our worldly enjoyments. Gill makes the same observation from the text's own phrasing: the plenty was in some measure known while the stores lasted, but before the seven years had run there were no traces of the former abundance to be seen.

Calvin closes on the doubling. Joseph does not mean that a thing God had declared only once would be changeable; he means to keep Pharaoh's confidence in the event from being shaken. Since God pronounces nothing except from his own fixed and steadfast purpose, it is enough that he should have spoken once, and it is our dullness and inconstancy that make him repeat the same thing more often, so that what he has certainly decreed may be fixed in our hearts. Otherwise, our disposition being variable, what we have once heard from his mouth is tossed up and down in us until it escapes the memory altogether. And Joseph adds that the thing is near at hand, lest the king should slumber in expectation of a longer delay; for though we confess that God's judgments hang over our heads, unless we are stirred by the thought of their speedy approach we are but slightly moved with anxiety about them.
33:
Having read the dream, Joseph goes on to advise, and every voice notices that he was not asked to. Calvin makes it a mark of office: Joseph is not merely the interpreter but fulfils the part of a prophet, since the true prophets of God never barely predict what is coming but propose remedies for impending evils, and God distinguished his own from the false prognosticators by endowing them with the power of teaching and exhorting. Grant that the oracles of Apollo and of the magicians were true; whither did they tend, except to drive men into perverse confidence or into despair? Because this prophecy concerned only the present life, Joseph goes no further than showing the king why the dream was sent.

Whether the counsel was inspired or simply shrewd is left open. Clarke argues that since Joseph could not have foreseen his own elevation, the advice had no reference to himself, and was either immediately inspired by God or dictated by sound policy. Gill will not have Joseph meaning himself either: it is scarcely consistent with his modesty, and he ventured no advice till asked. Calvin agrees that no craft was at work. Joseph did not insinuate himself into favour nor turn the gift of revelation to private gain; God guided his tongue so that Pharaoh should entrust him with the office, and what had been ordained was brought to its issue without his knowledge — that the famishing house of Jacob should find unexpected sustenance.

Henry takes the advice as a pattern for ordinary prudence. Fair warning should always be followed with good counsel: the prudent man foresees the evil and hides himself, and since God has told us of a day of trial ahead, we should provide accordingly. He also sees the administrative point. Because what is everybody's business commonly proves nobody's, Joseph advises that officers be appointed who shall make it their work, and one man set over the whole; had he not advised it, it probably would not have been done, since Pharaoh's counsellors could no more improve the dream than his magicians could interpret it — whence the psalm says that Joseph taught the senators wisdom, and one may justly infer with Solomon that better is a poor and wise child than an old and foolish king.

On the tax itself the commentators are close but not identical. Clarke renders the word for officers as visitors or overseers, and reports Ainsworth's bolder translation, bishops. The fifth part he identifies with the share still claimed by the crown in his own day, supposing the ordinary levy was more likely a tenth; but as the earth was bringing forth by handfuls, the king was justified in requiring a fifth, which out of such abundance the people could pay without feeling it oppressive. Ellicott reads the Hebrew as let him fifth the land, agrees that a tithe was probably the custom, and adds that since the reason for the enactment would be published it would induce careful people to lay up their own surplus too, and that the fifth was afterwards fixed as the king's rent. Gill notes that the corn was deposited in the cities against a time of public distress, the Targum saying it was hidden in a cave in the earth.

Calvin explains why the stores had to be under authority at all. Prosperity so intoxicates men that most make no provision for the future but absorb the present abundance by intemperance, and the bridle of authority was necessary because luxury wastes the blessings of God. Yet the granaries would also teach: seeing that so much corn was not gathered by the king for nothing, but as a remedy against some unwonted calamity, the common people would form habits of frugality themselves. So the dream proved useful after all, since the means of cure were suggested immediately after the wound had been shown.
37:
The counsel pleases: Gill notes that Pharaoh approved both the advice and the plan, Clarke that king and courtiers alike saw it was prudent. But the verdict Pharaoh pronounces on the man — one in whom the Spirit of God is — draws the closer notice. Clarke points out that the phrase is word for word the one used at the creation, and must be understood here as it is there; the Egyptians, idolaters though they were, acknowledged Joseph's God, since the knowledge of the true God was in Egypt long before, yet they might still have their gods many. Ellicott ties the compliment back to Joseph's disclaimer: having refused any art of divination and referred the answer to God, he is now recognised as the instrument through whom God had spoken, and as a man whose counsel, no less than his interpretation, marked him out for the work.

Calvin turns the appointment into a lesson on appointments generally. Ordinarily men are advanced because they are favourites, so that the unworthy creep in and ambition subverts equity; but necessity extorts a sober judgment, and Pharaoh says nothing that is not engraved on the hearts of all men, that honours belong only to competent persons whom God has furnished for them. Here his pride was subdued, so that he preferred a foreigner just out of prison to all his courtiers, and the same necessity restrained the nobles from their usual contest for precedence — a compulsory modesty, since they were ashamed to resist the public good. He notes too that a king infatuated by soothsayers still honours the gifts of the Spirit, because God never lets men grow so brutish as to feel nothing of his power. Gill supplies the human undercurrent: if any of the servants disliked the choice, through envy or through wanting the post themselves, they dared not oppose it.

The office itself is described by its reach. Ellicott notes that the chief over the palace stood next in power to the sovereign, and recalls that under the Frankish kings the mayor of the palace usurped the royal power and at last took the royal name. The clause about the people is the hard one. Its verb ordinarily means to kiss, so that the sense would be that they should do homage at his mouth; but because the same verb is used elsewhere of bearing arms, Aben Ezra translates that they shall arm themselves and makes Joseph commander-in-chief, while others render that the people shall busy themselves at his command. Ellicott prefers the first. Clarke agrees on the kiss, explaining from the eastern custom of kissing whatever comes from a superior, and calls the sentence a perfect description of a prime minister. Calvin also keeps the kiss, declining to twist a plain verb, but finds in it no particular ceremony; he reads it as a metaphor, that the people should cordially receive whatever proceeded from Joseph's mouth.

Calvin alone asks whether such elevation was safe for a holy man to accept. Joseph is not merely made governor but adorned with the insignia of royalty: the signet for confirming decrees, the fine linen that was then a luxury not to be had at any common price, the most honourable chariot. Was it lawful for him to appear in so much pomp? Such splendour, Calvin answers, can scarcely ever be quite free from blame, and frugality is best; yet not every magnificence in princes is to be condemned, provided it is neither eagerly desired nor ostentatiously displayed. It was not in Joseph's power to prescribe his own investiture, and the royal authority would not have been granted without the accustomed pomp of state, so he was at liberty to accept more than was in itself desirable. Where the option is given to the servants of God, nothing is safer than to cut off whatever outward splendour they can.
41:
The insignia are described piece by piece. Keil and Delitzsch identify the ring as the seal the grand vizier wore to give authority to royal edicts, and Ellicott observes that since decrees became law when stamped with it, it was naturally the symbol of power, as the great seal is still delivered into the hands of a new minister. Gill recalls that a ring marked admission to the Roman equestrian order and could also designate a successor, as when Alexander on his deathbed gave his to Perdiccas, though he does not suppose Pharaoh meant any such thing here. Clarke makes Joseph in effect Lord Keeper of the Privy Seal.

The linen is harder. Clarke cannot decide whether the word means linen or cotton; if it was the stuff that wraps the mummies, he says, it is fine only comparatively, for he had often examined the cloth about the most splendidly ornamented of them and found it sackcloth beside good Irish linen, though as part of the royal clothing it was probably both scarce and costly. Ellicott calls the word Egyptian and makes it a flax yielding linen of great fineness and whiteness, the same used for much of the priestly dress, and finds a further significance in the gift: changes of raiment are the usual mark of royal favour in the East, but white linen being the wear of kings and priests, this robing marked Joseph's admission to the ruling classes, and he was probably enrolled among the priesthood before his marriage. The gold chain, Ellicott says, appears on the monuments among the royal insignia, the surviving necklaces so exquisite that jewellers still copy their patterns. Clarke will have it stand for more than a badge of office: it may point out the union of king, ministers and people and their necessary dependence on one another, its gold denoting the excellence and permanence of a government founded on wise and equal laws — a reading he defends on the ground that in antiquity everything was made an emblem of something moral.

Then the procession, and a word that defeats everybody. The cry raised before the second chariot Clarke declares probably Egyptian and its meaning utterly unknown, though if it were Hebrew it might be compounded of father and tender, since Joseph was a father to the people in his care for them and tender in his youth, or of father and blessing, since he was turning aside the heavy curse of the famine by heaping up the blessings of the plenty; father, he adds, seems in any case to have been a name of office. Keil and Delitzsch also treat the word as Egyptian, but point to a Coptic term for casting down, and so keep the sense bow down, describing a solemn procession through the city with heralds crying it before him. Ellicott follows Canon Cook in reading it instead as rejoice, be happy: it stands in the imperative singular, and the text says the multitude cried it rather than a herald, so it was addressed to Joseph as a vivat rex, and its resemblance to the Hebrew for bow the knee is mere chance. He adds that the object of the whole parade was to display the new governor to the people, Pharaoh probably taking the chief part in the first chariot of state. Gill infers from the second chariot only what it was meant to show, that Joseph stood next to the king but not above him, kings keeping several chariots of graduated state.
44:
Pharaoh's last word settles the constitution of the thing. Gill and Clarke both hear in I am Pharaoh simply I am the king, the word being a title of office and not a personal name, and Gill takes the declaration either as reserving the crown or as asserting the authority by which the appointment was made and would be maintained. Keil and Delitzsch put it in one sentence: I am the actual king, and thou, next to me, shalt rule my people. Wesley reads the repetition as evidence of resistance — all the affairs of the kingdom must pass through Joseph's hand, and it is probable there were those at court who opposed his preferment, which is why Pharaoh so often repeats the grant with that solemn sanction.

The new name divides the commentators sharply. Gill reports the Targums for one to whom hidden things are revealed, and says most of the Jewish writers follow them, the name being given from the interpreting of the dreams; but he notes that the word occurs nowhere else, that Aben Ezra could not say whether it was Egyptian, and that some detect the name of an Egyptian idol in its first syllable, Pharaoh inserting his god's name as Nebuchadnezzar did when he renamed Daniel. Keil and Delitzsch prefer a Coptic derivation yielding sustainer of life, while recording the older Greek and Latin tradition of saviour of the world, and add that the naming and the marriage together were meant to naturalise Joseph completely. Ellicott takes it for food of life, or food of the living, and treats saviour of the world as a gloss meaning the same thing if the world means the living; there is, he says flatly, no authority for revealer of secrets. Clarke reckons every etymology doubtful, dismisses the Vulgate's rendering as arbitrary, and supposes the word an Egyptian title of office like Prime Minister or Lord Chancellor.

The marriage raises the last difficulty. Clarke denies that Joseph's father-in-law can be the Potiphar who had bought him, since scripture nowhere hints it and this man had children while the other was a eunuch, and he identifies On with Heliopolis. Ellicott makes On the Egyptian word for the sun, whence the Hebrew and Greek names of the city, and describes its temple of Ra, destroyed early by the Persians but still marked by an obelisk of extreme antiquity. He then meets the objection that a Hebrew shepherd should marry a sun-priest's daughter: the raising of a slave to rank is not uncommon in the East, where slaves might be of as good birth as their owners; no high priest would refuse a daughter to the king's favourite; and the narrative everywhere shows Joseph faithful to the religion of his family, whose God Pharaoh himself acknowledges, though on public occasions he would have had to attend the Egyptian solemnities, whose creed still held much primeval truth in a corrupted form. He points as well to an Egyptian tale older than Joseph, of a foreigner who entered the country in the dress of a herb-seller, married a local king's daughter, and was at last clothed in kingly attire. Keil and Delitzsch read the wife's name as connected with the Egyptian Neith and the father's as one who belongs to the sun. Clarke takes the closing words to mean that Joseph toured the whole land to build granaries and appoint the officers who were to receive the corn.

Wesley closes on what the honours were for. Where God had been liberal in giving wisdom, Pharaoh was not sparing in conferring honours; and the preferment was both an abundant recompense for innocent and patient suffering and a type of the exaltation of Christ, that great revealer of secrets — or, as some render the new name, the saviour of the world — who is gatherer, keeper and disposer of all the stores of divine grace.
46:
The stated age invites arithmetic. Joseph was seventeen when he was sold and thirty when he stood before Pharaoh, so Gill counts thirteen years in Egypt, partly in Potiphar's house and partly in prison; Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch reach the same figure, the latter adding that at least three of those years were in the prison. Clarke also notes the force of the phrase: to stand before a sovereign means admission to his immediate presence and unlimited confidence, granted among Eastern princes only to the highest favourites.

Calvin finds two reasons for recording the age at all. The first is that old men seldom submit to be governed by the young, so it was by a singular providence that Joseph ruled without being envied and that a reverence beyond his years was granted him; if there was danger that Timothy's youth would make him contemptible, Joseph stood equally exposed unless authority had been divinely procured for him. The second is that the reader may weigh how long his sufferings ran: thirteen years of exile that kept him from his father's house, by servitude first and then by imprisonment, was a most grievous trial, and only after such long endurance was he advanced.

Then Calvin turns to how the office was discharged. The circuit Joseph made through the land was proof of no common industry: he might have laid the greater part of the labour on other shoulders, but knowing himself divinely called, and accountable to the divine tribunal, he refused no part of the burden. His prudence Calvin calls incredible, since it was an arduous business to erect storehouses in every city capable of holding a year's produce and a fifth more, and no small sagacity to arrange that no region should have to seek food at a distance. His integrity was equal to it, for amid an immense accumulation he abstained from all self-indulgence. And both virtues appear in this, that after the heaps were gathered he remitted nothing of his diligence. The old proverb says that satiety produces disgust, and abundance is commonly the mother of idleness; whence then did Joseph's diligence hold its even course, except that he considered that seven years of famine would swallow it all?

Henry reads the same stretch as a stewardship faithfully kept. Joseph was diligent in laying up while the plenty lasted, and he that thus gathers is a wise son; and he adds the rule, that we ought to foresee the end of the days both of our prosperity and of our opportunity, being neither secure in the one nor slothful in the other. Years of plenty will end: gather in gathering time.

The description of the harvest itself puzzles the commentators pleasantly. Gill takes the phrase from what reapers take up in their hands to bind into sheaves, and reports the rabbinic readings that one stalk bore as many ears as a man could hold, or that a single grain yielded a handful, alongside the Targum's different paraphrase that the inhabitants gathered into their treasuries. Keil and Delitzsch render it in full hands or bundles. Clarke thinks it refers principally to rice, which grows in tufts with many stalks springing from one seed. What was gathered was the levied fifth, stored city by city; Keil and Delitzsch describe granaries provided in the towns to hold the corn of the surrounding country, and note that the reckoning was given up when the quantity passed counting, as the monuments show was usual. Gill is careful about the title: not everything eatable but the corn, and only the fifth part of that, bought with Pharaoh's money, which is precisely why he had the right to sell it again. Ellicott suspects the stores were larger than the tax alone, since the fifth had also to meet the expenses of the realm, and supposes Joseph bought corn largely while it stood cheapest.
50:
Two sons are born before the famine, and their names are the whole of the comment. Clarke derives them plainly — the first from the verb to forget, the second from the verb to be fruitful — and reads both as expressive of God's particular and bountiful providence, since God had enabled Joseph to forget all his toil, disgrace and affliction, and had made him fruitful in the very land where he had suffered his greatest misfortunes and indignities. Gill notes that the verb for their birth stands in the singular, from which one Jewish commentator conjectured that they were twins, and observes that the second name is of dual form, which may take in both the spiritual and the temporal fruitfulness God had given him. Ellicott agrees that the dual ending probably intensifies the sense, and Keil and Delitzsch render it double fruitfulness.

The difficulty is in what the first name says. Joseph declares that God has made him forget all his toil and all his father's house, and the voices divide sharply over that last clause. Wesley states the problem without resolving it: Joseph owned divine providence in giving this happy turn to his affairs, and was made to forget his misery — but could he be so unnatural as to forget all his father's house? He notes too that the second name still calls Egypt the land of his affliction, and that in some sense it remained so, for his distance from his father was an affliction yet.

Calvin will not soften it. The names breathe piety, he grants, since in them Joseph celebrates the kindness of God, and it was a holy motive of gratitude that God had made him forget his former miseries; but no honour ought ever to have been valued so highly as to displace from a man's mind the desire and remembrance of his father's house. Grant that he is viceroy of Egypt: his condition is still unhappy while he remains an exile from the Church. The attempt of some to clear him, by explaining that he so rejoiced in God's present favour as to forget the injuries his brethren had done him, Calvin judges far too forced. We must not labour anxiously to excuse the sin of a holy man, he says; we should rather be admonished how carefully we ought to guard against the attractions of the world, lest our minds be unduly gratified by them. Behold Joseph, who worships God purely, so captivated by the sweetness of honour and so clouded in mind that he grows indifferent to his father's house and pleases himself in Egypt — which was almost to wander out of the fold of God. Yet Calvin finds one thing becoming even here: those who are raised from an obscure position commonly wish to extinguish all knowledge of their origin as a disgrace, whereas Joseph, wanting to proclaim the divine goodness toward him, was not ashamed to make his sons' names a perpetual memorial of his low estate, valuing the commendation of grace above an ostentatious nobility.

Ellicott answers the charge directly. Joseph has been blamed for forgetting his father's house, he says, but the phrase means only that now he was married and had a child he ceased to suffer from homesickness and grew contented with his lot; he no longer pined for the open downs of Canaan as he had done in the prison, and his love for his father was as warm as ever. Keil and Delitzsch take a middle path by attending to the other name: even after his elevation Egypt is still called the land of his affliction, and in that word they see one surviving trace of a longing for the promised land.
53:
The plenty ends and the prediction is verified. Gill supposes the change came soon after the birth of the second son, and describes the first signs: the river failing to reach its usual height, the earth parched, the seed not springing up. Clarke traces it to the Nile rising no more than twelve or thirteen cubits, but insists other causes were at work, since countries not dependent on the river suffered too. Wesley says the dearth was not only in Egypt but in all the neighbouring countries. Keil and Delitzsch add the meteorology: such years have often fallen on Egypt and the lands north of it, because the inundation is fed by rain in the highlands of Abyssinia.

Ellicott presses the historical setting. At this period the overflow was not yet regulated by dams and canals, so famines were far commoner than after the kings had guarded against the danger; and since the dearth reached Arabia, Palestine and Ethiopia, there was plainly a long drought. He cites a chronicler's account of a later Egyptian famine in which one city that had counted three hundred thousand poll-tax payers the year before was left with fewer than a hundred souls, and reports the argument that Joseph's Pharaoh first built the system of dykes and reservoirs.

Calvin is interested in the politics. The fertility of the good years had already made Joseph a name, and so restrained the Egyptians from tumult; still, it is wonderful that so proud a people bore a foreigner's rule in prosperity, and the famine proved a severer curb for subduing their ferocious spirits. He notices too the phrasing that there was bread in all the land of Egypt, and infers that private persons must also have laid up wheat, since the rumour of a famine could not but spread. Yet what they preserved would soon be consumed; and from that it appears how clearly Joseph had seen that Egypt would not be safe unless the provisions were publicly gathered under the king's hand. Clarke reaches the opposite estimate: since a fifth had been exacted throughout the plenty, no more was likely left than served ordinary demand.

When the people cry to Pharaoh he sends them to Joseph, and Calvin will not read this as royal indolence. It is common enough for kings to give themselves to pleasure while their subjects are in extremity, but that is not the meaning here: Pharaoh leaves the distribution to Joseph out of such confidence that he will not have him hindered in his office. Keil and Delitzsch add that Joseph opened all the granaries and dealt in corn with Egyptians and foreigners alike. On the reach of the famine Gill and Clarke both restrain the language: the phrase covering the face of the earth means the face of that land, so that all the inhabitants of Egypt were pinched by it, while the neighbouring nations came for corn, since none was to be had elsewhere.

Two closing reflections stand out. Gill reports the opinion of many that the Egyptians afterwards worshipped Joseph, in gratitude for the care that preserved them, under several of their own divine names — the ox that signified fruitfulness, and the gods figured with a basket of bread or a measure upon the head — but rests on what he holds certain, that Joseph was an eminent type of Christ, falsely accused and bound as Christ was. Clarke ends with providence and dreams. The same providence that led the butler, the baker and the king to dream led the Spirit in Joseph to interpret truly — a providence general enough to reach every part and particular enough to direct the smallest circumstance. Dreams he divides into six kinds, from the nightly residue of the day's business to those that come immediately from God, adding that there is often as much superstition in disregarding them as in heeding them.
